Drug Targets enzymes, receptors & transporters

Almost every drug works by touching one of four proteins. This guide merges both Week-5 lectures — how drugs bend enzymes, the four receptor superfamilies, and transporters as targets — decoding the deck's own figures and adding the mechanism behind each.

Covers L9 (Enzymes & Receptors) + L10 (Receptors & Transporters), 49 slides Figures from the MEDI2004 decks Self-tests interactive

§0The big picture · L9 slide 3 / L10 slide 22

What is a drug target?

Four protein classes; three things a drug can do to each.

Before any single drug makes sense, learn the map. The overwhelming majority of drugs act on just four classes of protein — receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers) — and on any of them a drug does one of only three things: it can activate, inhibit/block, or modulate the target. Hold that grid in your head and every later example (a nerve gas, an antidepressant, an anticancer drug) becomes a variation on the same theme. The rest of this guide walks the grid: enzymes (§1), receptors (§2) and transporters (§3), with ion channels appearing as the fastest kind of receptor.

Label Key — the four targets (A–D)
A · Receptors
An agonist binds and triggers a transduction mechanism — opening/closing a channel, activating/inhibiting an enzyme, or driving DNA transcription. An antagonist occupies the receptor with no effect, so it blocks endogenous mediators. Matters because it is the difference between adding a signal and removing one.
B · Ion channels
Blockers physically stop ion permeation through the pore; modulators increase or decrease the channel's opening probability without plugging it. Matters because modulation lets a drug fine-tune, not just switch off.
C · Enzymes
An inhibitor blocks the normal reaction; a false substrate is accepted by the enzyme and turned into an abnormal metabolite. Matters because a false substrate hijacks the enzyme's own catalysis against the pathway.
D · Transporters
An inhibitor blocks transport through the carrier; a false substrate is carried across so an abnormal compound accumulates inside. Matters because it explains both reuptake inhibitors and toxic accumulation.

Read Plate 0.1 as a two-by-two menu. Down each panel the top row is the "on" action (agonist/normal transport), the middle rows are the drug interventions (inhibit, modulate, false substrate), and the arrows on the right name the consequence. Notice the recurring pair — an inhibitor that simply stops the process, versus a false substrate that is processed into something abnormal. That distinction (block vs. corrupt) returns for both enzymes and transporters.

Reasoning · why only four classes?

These four are the proteins that convert a chemical signal into a cellular action: receptors read messengers, ion channels set membrane excitability, enzymes run metabolism, and transporters move solutes across membranes. A drug is just a small molecule; to change physiology it has to grab a protein that already controls a step. Structural (skeletal) or bulk proteins make poor targets because binding them changes little downstream — so the druggable proteome collapses onto these four functional classes.

Memory hook · RITE targets, AIM actions

Targets = R.I.T.E. — Receptors, Ion channels, Transporters, Enzymes. Actions = A.I.M. — Activate, Inhibit, Modulate. Every drug in the unit is one RITE target hit by one AIM action.

Clinical / real-world

The grid predicts side-effect logic. A drug that blocks an enzyme (e.g. an ACE inhibitor) removes a product; a drug that is a false substrate (e.g. methyldopa, made into a false transmitter) produces an abnormal molecule that itself has actions. Knowing which square a drug sits in tells you whether toxicity comes from loss of the normal product or from gain of an abnormal one.

R Recall checklist — the target map
  • Four target classes — receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters.
  • Three actions — activate, inhibit/block, modulate.
  • Agonist vs antagonist — agonist triggers transduction; antagonist occupies with no effect and blocks the endogenous mediator.
  • Inhibitor vs false substrate — one stops the process, the other is processed into an abnormal product.
§1L9 slides 4–8 · Objective: how drugs affect enzymes

Enzymes as drug targets

Catalysts you can block, or feed the wrong molecule.

Enzymes are biological catalysts — powerful and highly specific. Each one accelerates a single chemical reaction and comes out unchanged, so a small amount of enzyme turns over a large amount of substrate. Chains of these reactions build the body's metabolic pathways (anabolic = synthesis; catabolic = breakdown), and by convention their names end in -ase. Because one enzyme gates one step, blocking it is a precise way to redirect physiology — which is exactly what many drugs do.

Label Key — the catalytic cycle
Substrate(s)
The reactant molecule(s) the enzyme acts on. They must fit the active site — this is the source of an enzyme's specificity, and the site a drug competes for.
Active site
The pocket where catalysis happens. Its shape decides which substrate binds; drugs that occupy it (competitive inhibitors, false substrates) work here.
Enzyme–substrate complex
The transient bound state in which the reaction is catalysed. Lowering the energy needed to reach it is how the enzyme speeds the reaction.
Product + free enzyme
The reaction output is released and the enzyme is regenerated unchanged, ready to cycle again — which is why a little enzyme does a lot of work, and why irreversible inhibition is so potent (it removes a reusable catalyst).

As Plate 1.1 shows, the enzyme is a reusable machine: substrate in, product out, enzyme back to start. A drug can jam this cycle in two ways — sit in the active site so the true substrate cannot bind (an inhibitor), or slip in as a false substrate and be turned into the wrong product. We meet both below, using acetylcholine as the worked biological example.

Label Key — acetylcholine handling (steps 1–6)
Choline + Acetyl-CoA
The two building blocks. Choline acetyltransferase joins them into ACh (step 1) — the synthetic enzyme, itself a potential drug target.
Acetylcholine (ACh)
The transmitter, packaged into vesicles (step 2) and released into the synapse (step 3). Its lifetime in the cleft sets the size of the signal.
Synapse
The gap ACh crosses (step 3) to reach the far side.
Receptor
The postsynaptic target ACh binds to send the message (step 4). Sustained by drugs that stop ACh breakdown.
Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)
The degrading enzyme (step 6): it hydrolyses ACh to terminate the signal. This is the drug target — inhibit it and ACh lingers, amplifying cholinergic transmission.

Trace the arrows in Plate 1.2: two enzymes bracket the transmitter's life — one makes ACh (choline acetyltransferase, step 1) and one destroys it (acetylcholinesterase, step 6). Drugs cluster on the destroyer, because slowing breakdown is an easy way to raise a transmitter without having to synthesise or inject it.

Reasoning · why target the breakdown enzyme, not the synthesis one?

Inhibiting AChE raises ACh only where and when ACh is already being released — the drug amplifies the existing physiological signal rather than flooding every synapse. Blocking synthesis instead would silence transmission everywhere and could not be dialled by activity. This "amplify what's happening" logic is why esterase inhibitors are useful in conditions of too little cholinergic signalling (Alzheimer's, myasthenia gravis).

§1.1Anticholinesterases: reversible vs irreversible

Anticholinesterase drugs inhibit AChE, but they split into two mechanistic camps with very different safety profiles. Reversible inhibitors bind AChE transiently and let go — these are the therapeutic drugs: donepezil and rivastigmine (Alzheimer's disease) and pyridostigmine (myasthenia gravis). Irreversible inhibitors form an essentially permanent bond and are poisons: organophosphate nerve agents such as sarin gas and insecticides such as parathion.

Reversible vs irreversible AChE inhibitors
FeatureReversibleIrreversible
BindingTransient — enzyme recoversCovalent/near-permanent — enzyme lost until resynthesised
ExamplesDonepezil, rivastigmine, pyridostigmineSarin (nerve agent), parathion (insecticide)
Use / hazardTherapeutic: Alzheimer's, myasthenia gravisToxic: chemical warfare, poisoning
Duration of effectSet by the drug's dwell time / dosingOutlasts the drug — needs new enzyme (or an antidote)
Clinical / real-world

The same mechanism — more synaptic ACh — is a treatment at low reversible doses and a lethal toxidrome when irreversible. Organophosphate poisoning floods muscarinic and nicotinic synapses, giving the SLUDGE picture (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis) plus bronchospasm and, ultimately, respiratory failure. Treatment mirrors the mechanism: atropine blocks the muscarinic receptors downstream, and pralidoxime can prise the organophosphate off AChE if given before the bond "ages" — a direct application of reversible-vs-irreversible chemistry.

Memory hook · gas is forever

Nerve gas and pesticides bind irreversibly (they "gas" the enzyme for good); the "-stigmine/-zil" medicines let go. If it treats a disease it's reversible; if it's a weapon it's not.

§1.2False substrates: methotrexate & fluorouracil

A false substrate is a drug molecule that the enzyme accepts and chemically transforms into an abnormal product, while also competing with the true substrate for the binding site — so it corrupts a metabolic pathway from two directions at once. The classic anticancer example targets folate/thymidine metabolism, the supply line for DNA synthesis.

Label Key — the folate/thymidylate cycle
DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase)
Regenerates active (reduced) folate needed to donate one-carbon units. Methotrexate inhibits it (the two ⊖ symbols), starving the cell of usable folate.
Thymidylate synthetase
Converts dUMP → dTMP, the DNA base thymidylate. Fluorouracil (5-FU) inhibits it (bottom ⊖), blocking thymidine (and thus DNA) synthesis.
FH₂ / FH₄ (glu)ₙ
Dihydro- and tetrahydrofolate pools that carry one-carbon units. Their depletion is the downstream consequence of DHFR inhibition.
dTMP / dUMP
Thymidylate and its precursor. Falling dTMP is the point of attack — no thymidylate, no DNA replication in dividing cells.

Follow the two red drugs in Plate 1.3: methotrexate clamps the enzyme (DHFR) that keeps folate recycled, and fluorouracil clamps thymidylate synthetase one step later. Both choke the same output — the thymidylate a cell needs to copy its DNA. Because tumour cells divide fast and demand DNA precursors, they are hit hardest.

Reasoning · why hitting one pathway twice works

DNA synthesis is a supply chain: block folate recycling (methotrexate) and the thymidylate-forming step (fluorouracil) and you cut the line at two points, making escape harder. Targeting a metabolic bottleneck that dividing cells rely on is the whole logic of antimetabolite chemotherapy — the drugs look enough like the natural substrate to enter the active site, but the enzyme cannot complete its normal job.

Clinical / real-world

Because these drugs starve any fast-dividing tissue, their toxicities are predictable from the mechanism: bone-marrow suppression, mucositis and GI epithelial damage. Methotrexate toxicity can be rescued with folinic acid (leucovorin), which bypasses the blocked DHFR step — a rescue that only makes sense once you see methotrexate as a folate-pathway false substrate/inhibitor. Methotrexate is also used at low dose as an immunosuppressant (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis), exploiting the same antiproliferative effect on immune cells.

Worked example · why an irreversible AChE inhibitor outlasts the drug in the blood

A reversible inhibitor's effect tracks how much drug is bound, which follows occupancy: occupancy = [D] / ([D] + KD). An irreversible inhibitor breaks this link. Suppose an organophosphate has fully inactivated a person's AChE, and AChE is replaced by new synthesis at ~1% per hour. Estimate how long until enzyme activity returns to ~50% if no antidote is given.

  1. State the model. Reversible drugs obey occupancy — remove the drug and effect fades within a few half-lives. Irreversible inhibition destroys the enzyme, so recovery depends on enzyme resynthesis, not on clearing the drug.
  2. Set up recovery. If active enzyme is regenerated at a constant ~1% of the normal pool per hour, activity climbs roughly linearly at first: activity ≈ rate × time.
  3. Substitute. To reach 50% at ~1%/hour: time ≈ 50% ÷ 1%·h⁻¹ = 50 h.
  4. Interpret. That is ~2 days of impaired cholinergic transmission even after the poison itself has been cleared — the clinical hallmark of irreversible inhibition, and the reason pralidoxime (which reactivates the enzyme) must be given early, before the bond "ages" beyond rescue.

Answer: ≈ 50 hours to half-recovery — effect is set by enzyme resynthesis, not drug clearance. (Reversible inhibitors, by contrast, recover within a few drug half-lives.)

R Recall checklist — enzymes as targets
  • Enzymes — specific, reusable catalysts; names end in -ase; substrate → E-S complex → product + free enzyme.
  • ACh cycle — choline acetyltransferase makes it, acetylcholinesterase breaks it (the drug target).
  • Anticholinesterases — reversible = donepezil / rivastigmine / pyridostigmine (therapeutic); irreversible = sarin / parathion (toxic).
  • False substrate — processed into an abnormal product AND competes with substrate.
  • Antimetabolites — methotrexate ⟂ DHFR; fluorouracil ⟂ thymidylate synthetase; both block DNA synthesis.
§2L9 slides 9–23 + L10 slides 3–14 · Objective: the four superfamilies

Receptors — the four superfamilies

One idea, four architectures, four timescales.

Receptors are protein molecules that, when activated by transmitters, hormones or drugs, mediate a biological effect — they are how cells listen to chemical signals from other cells and coordinate the body. All receptors share that job, but they come in four superfamilies that differ in location, effector, coupling and structure — the four axes you are asked to compare. The single most powerful organising fact: the speed of a receptor follows its mechanism, from milliseconds to hours.

Label Key — the four types, left to right
1 · Ligand-gated ion channel
Ionotropic. Ligand opens a channel → ions flow → hyperpolarisation or depolarisation → cellular effect. Direct coupling, milliseconds — the fastest.
2 · GPCR (metabotropic)
Ligand → G-protein → change in excitability or second messengers (Ca²⁺ release, protein phosphorylation) → cellular effect. Seconds.
3 · Kinase-linked receptor
Ligand → receptor/enzyme (R/E) → protein phosphorylation → gene transcription → protein synthesis → effect. Hours.
4 · Nuclear receptor
Ligand crosses the membrane → binds an intracellular receptor in the nucleus → gene transcription → protein synthesis → effect. Hours.
Time-scale row
Milliseconds → seconds → hours → hours. The take-home: anything that needs gene transcription is slow; direct ion flow is fast.

Plate 2.1 is the spine of this section — every subsection below zooms into one of its four columns. Read the bottom time-scale row first: the two right-hand types are slow precisely because their output is new protein, which takes transcription and translation, whereas an ion channel just lets ions through. That single insight lets you predict a receptor's tempo from its wiring.

Reasoning · why speed tracks mechanism

The number of steps between ligand and effect sets the delay. A ligand-gated channel converts binding directly into ion flux — one step, milliseconds. A GPCR inserts a G-protein and a second messenger — a few steps, seconds. Kinase-linked and nuclear receptors must reach the genome and wait for transcription and protein synthesis — many steps, hours. So "how fast?" and "how is it coupled?" are the same question.

Memory hook · "I Get Kinda Nervous"

Ionotropic → GPCR → Kinase-linked → Nuclear = "I Get Kinda Nervous", in order of increasing time-scale (ms → s → hours → hours).

Clinical / real-world

The timescale sets how a drug is used. A fast ionotropic target suits emergencies (a neuromuscular blocker paralyses in seconds via nicotinic channels); a nuclear-receptor drug such as a glucocorticoid takes hours to reach full effect because it must change gene expression — which is why steroids are given ahead of need, not for instant relief.

§2.1Type 1 · Ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic)

Examples are the nicotinic ACh, GABAA and NMDA receptors. Also called ionotropic receptors, they sit mostly in the cell membrane (some also in intracellular membranes such as the endoplasmic reticulum) and are built as an oligomeric assembly of ~4–5 subunits surrounding a central pore. Their effector is the ion channel itself (direct coupling), so they control the fastest synaptic events in the nervous system (millisecond timescale).

Label Key — GABA_A architecture & pharmacology
Cl⁻ pore
The central channel. Opening lets chloride in, hyperpolarising the neuron — this is inhibition, the basis of anxiolysis and sedation.
α / β / γ subunits (with M1–M4)
Five subunits (typically 2α, 2β, 1γ; from α1–6, β1–3, γ1–3 or δ,ε,θ,π) each cross the membrane four times (M1–M4). Subunit composition tunes the receptor's pharmacology.
GABA site
The orthosteric site (at α/β interfaces) where GABA binds to open the channel — the natural "on" switch.
BZ (benzodiazepine) site
An allosteric site (α/γ interface): benzodiazepines bind here and increase the channel's response to GABA — enhancing inhibition without opening the channel themselves.
Barbiturate site
A separate allosteric site; barbiturates prolong channel opening and at high dose can open it directly — hence their narrower safety margin.
Neurosteroid (NS) sites
Allosteric and direct sites for neurosteroids, another modulatory input — showing one channel can be tuned from several independent sites.

Plate 2.2 makes the "modulator" idea from §0 concrete: GABA opens the pore from its own orthosteric site, while benzodiazepines, barbiturates and neurosteroids each bind allosterically and change how well GABA works. Because these are separate sites on the same ring of subunits, several drug classes can act on one channel — the molecular reason a benzodiazepine and a barbiturate interact.

Label Key — where drugs act (NMDA vs GABA_A)
NMDA · receptor site
Glutamate (+ co-agonist) binds here to open the channel; NMDA antagonists block it. The channel passes Na⁺ and Ca²⁺, making NMDA important in excitotoxicity and learning.
NMDA · modulatory sites
Glycine and polyamine sites tune the response (with their antagonists); Mg²⁺ blocks the pore at rest — a voltage-dependent plug.
NMDA · channel-blocking drugs
Bind inside the open pore (e.g. ketamine, memantine) — a physical block, exploited clinically and recreationally.
GABA_A · receptor site
GABA binds to open the Cl⁻ channel; GABA antagonists block it.
GABA_A · modulatory site
Benzodiazepine agonists enhance, antagonists block, and inverse agonists reduce GABA's effect; "channel modulators" act elsewhere on the pore — a full allosteric spectrum on one receptor.

Set Plate 2.3 beside Plate 2.2: both receptors have a receptor (orthosteric) site for the transmitter and separate modulatory and channel-blocking sites. The NMDA panel also shows the full agonist–antagonist–inverse agonist range at the benzodiazepine site — a preview of the "efficacy" ideas that recur across the superfamilies.

Reasoning · why an oligomer of 4–5 subunits?

Building the receptor from several subunits around a pore does two jobs at once. It creates a water-filled channel for ions to cross the membrane, and it generates multiple interfaces between subunits — each a potential binding site. That is why one GABAA receptor can host GABA, benzodiazepine, barbiturate and neurosteroid sites: the modular build is the pharmacology. Swapping one subunit (e.g. α1 vs α2) changes which drugs bind and how strongly.

Clinical / real-world

This is why benzodiazepines (diazepam) are relatively safe sedatives but barbiturates are dangerous: a benzodiazepine only enhances GABA and cannot open the channel alone, so there is a ceiling; a barbiturate can open the Cl⁻ channel directly at high dose, so overdose causes fatal respiratory depression. The benzodiazepine antidote flumazenil works because it is a competitive antagonist at that same allosteric site. On the NMDA side, memantine (Alzheimer's) and ketamine (anaesthetic/antidepressant) are channel blockers.

§2.2Type 2 · G-protein-coupled receptors (metabotropic)

Examples are the cannabinoid, opioid and adrenergic receptors. GPCRs — also called metabotropic or 7-transmembrane receptors — sit in the cell membrane and are built from seven transmembrane α-helices with an intracellular G-protein-coupling domain. They are slower than ion channels but faster than transcription-dependent receptors, and their effectors are channels or enzymes activated via G proteins or arrestins.

Label Key — the four states of the cycle
Resting state
Receptor empty; G-protein intact as α-GDP·βγ, targets inactive. The default "off".
Agonist bound → GDP/GTP exchange
Agonist occupies the receptor, which acts as a GEF: Gα releases GDP and binds GTP, then dissociates from βγ. This is the activation switch.
Targets activated
Free Gα-GTP and βγ each activate their targets (enzymes/channels) — one receptor can drive two effectors.
GTP hydrolysed (+Pᵢ)
The α-subunit's intrinsic GTPase hydrolyses GTP → GDP, so Gα re-associates with βγ and the system resets. The built-in off-switch.

Follow the loop in Plate 2.4 clockwise. The whole point is a timed switch: the receptor turns the G-protein on by swapping GDP for GTP, and the G-protein turns itself off by hydrolysing that GTP. Because the GTPase lives in the α subunit, the α subunit is both accelerator and brake — an elegant self-limiting design.

Label Key — push-pull on one enzyme
Inhibitory receptor → Gi
Couples through Gαi to inhibit the target enzyme (−). Explains how one transmitter can turn a pathway down.
Stimulatory receptor → Gs
Couples through Gαs to stimulate the same enzyme (+). The two inputs let a cell integrate opposing signals.
Target enzyme
Typically adenylyl cyclase (makes cAMP): Gαs raises cAMP, Gαi lowers it. Gαq instead activates phospholipase C → IP₃ + DAG; βγ gates Ca²⁺/K⁺ channels.

Plate 2.5 shows the payoff of the α-subunit family: the same target enzyme is pushed up by Gαs and pulled down by Gαi. Add Gαq (→ phospholipase C → IP3 + DAG) and the βγ subunits (→ Ca2+ and K+ channels), and a small set of G-proteins covers stimulation, inhibition and a second messenger arm.

Label Key — switching a GPCR off and moving it
GRK phosphorylation
A G-protein-coupled receptor kinase phosphorylates the agonist-occupied receptor — the tag that starts desensitisation.
β-arrestin binding
β-arrestin binds the phosphorylated receptor: it uncouples the G-protein (desensitisation) and triggers its own β-arrestin signalling.
Clathrin / dynamin internalisation
The receptor is drawn into a clathrin-coated pit and pinched off by dynamin into an endosome — removing it from the surface.
Recycling vs degradation
From the endosome the receptor is either recycled back to the membrane (resensitisation) or sent to the lysosome for degradation (down-regulation).

Plate 2.6 explains why sustained stimulation fades: GRK + β-arrestin uncouple and internalise the receptor. Crucially, β-arrestin is not just an "off" signal — it launches its own signalling, which is the structural basis for the biased agonism we meet in §2.6.

Reasoning · why desensitise at all?

A cell that could not turn down a persistent signal would be locked in one state. Phosphorylation-plus-arrestin gives a graded, reversible way to reduce responsiveness (desensitisation) and, over longer exposure, to physically remove receptors (down-regulation). This is homeostasis at the receptor level — and it directly produces drug tolerance.

Clinical / real-world

Receptor desensitisation/down-regulation is why opioid tolerance develops — chronic agonist drives internalisation, so a bigger dose is needed for the same effect. The flip side is up-regulation: chronic β-blockade increases β-receptor number, so abruptly stopping a beta-blocker can cause rebound tachycardia. GPCRs are the single largest drug-target class (≈ a third of all marketed drugs), so these principles underpin a huge slice of pharmacology.

§2.3Type 3 · Kinase-linked and related receptors

Examples are the receptors for insulin, growth factors and cytokines. Their agonists are protein mediators; they sit in the cell membrane (some intracellular) and have a large extracellular ligand-binding domain linked by a single transmembrane helix to an intracellular domain that in most cases is enzymatic (protein kinase or guanylyl cyclase activity). Ligand binding causes dimerisation, and activation ultimately alters gene transcription (a slow effect).

Label Key — RTK anatomy & switch-on
EGF binding site (extracellular)
The large domain that reads the growth-factor ligand. Its occupancy is what starts everything.
Single transmembrane helix
One pass through the membrane — contrast the seven of a GPCR. It simply relays the signal inward.
Tyrosine kinase (cytosolic tail)
The intracellular enzyme domain carrying tyrosine (Tyr) residues. This is the receptor's own catalytic activity — a direct effect, no G-protein needed.
Dimerisation → autophosphorylation (P)
Ligand brings two receptors together; the paired kinases phosphorylate each other's tyrosines (Tyr→P). Those phosphotyrosines are the docking sites that launch downstream signalling.

Plate 2.7 captures the defining move of this family: the ligand does not open a channel or nudge a G-protein — it makes two receptors pair up so their built-in kinases switch each other on. The phosphotyrosines created become a landing pad for the cascade in Plate 2.8.

Label Key — the Ras/MAP-kinase cascade
Grb2 (SH2 adaptor)
Docks onto the phosphotyrosines of the active receptor — the adaptor that links the receptor to Ras.
Ras (GTP/GDP)
A small G-protein switched to its active GTP form; a hub whose faults drive many cancers.
Raf → MEK → MAPK
A three-tier kinase cascade that amplifies the signal, each kinase phosphorylating the next (note the scaffold protein holding them together).
Transcription
MAPK enters the nucleus and switches on transcription factors — the slow, growth-and-proliferation output.
Label Key — JAK–STAT
Janus kinase (JAK)
An associated kinase (the receptor itself lacks enzyme activity here) that is activated when cytokine dimerises the receptor.
STAT
A latent transcription factor: JAK phosphorylates it, two STATs pair up, translocate to the nucleus and drive gene regulation.
SOCS
Suppressor of cytokine signalling — a negative feedback brake (−) on JAK, keeping the response self-limiting.

As Plate 2.9 shows, the cytokine receptor has no kinase of its own — dimerisation instead activates an associated Janus kinase, which phosphorylates STAT so it can pair up and travel to the nucleus, while SOCS supplies the self-limiting brake. Compare it with Plate 2.8: an RTK carries its own kinase and signals through Ras/MAPK, whereas the cytokine receptor borrows a separate JAK and signals through STATs — but both funnel to the nucleus to change transcription, which is why both are slow.

Reasoning · why dimerise?

A single kinase domain sitting quietly in the membrane is inert. Bringing two together (dimerisation) lets them phosphorylate each other — a clean way to convert "ligand present" into "kinase active" with no intermediate messenger. Trans-autophosphorylation also builds the phosphotyrosine docking sites the cascade needs, so one event (pairing) both switches the enzyme on and recruits its partners.

Clinical / real-world

These pathways are prime cancer and immune drug targets. Trastuzumab blocks the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase in breast cancer; imatinib inhibits the BCR-ABL kinase in CML; -tinib drugs inhibit RTKs broadly; and JAK inhibitors ("-tinib" e.g. tofacitinib) damp cytokine signalling in rheumatoid arthritis. Because the output is proliferation/transcription, effects and toxicities build over days, not minutes.

§2.4Type 4 · Nuclear (intracellular) receptors

Examples are the oestrogen, androgen, glucocorticoid and thyroid-hormone receptors. These are ligand-activated transcription factors that regulate gene transcription (slow action). They live in the cytoplasm (class I) or nucleus (class II); after ligand binds they form homo- or heterodimers, translocate to the nucleus, and the receptor–ligand complex binds hormone-response elements in gene promoters, recruiting co-activators or co-repressors to switch genes on or off.

Label Key — from lipophilic ligand to transcription
Steroid ligand (GC / A / E)
A lipophilic hormone (glucocorticoid, androgen, oestrogen) that crosses the membrane unaided — the reason these receptors can be intracellular.
HSP (heat-shock protein)
Chaperone holding a class-I receptor (AR/GR) inactive in the cytoplasm; ligand binding releases it, unmasking the receptor.
Receptor dimer → nucleus
The freed receptor dimerises and translocates into the nucleus — the slow, trafficking step.
SRE / hormone-response element
The specific DNA sequence the complex binds; recruiting co-regulators then turns transcription up or down (+/−).

In Plate 2.10 the ligand's lipophilicity is the whole story: because a steroid slips through the membrane, its receptor can wait inside the cell (on HSP, for class I) rather than at the surface. Binding releases the chaperone, the complex reaches the DNA, and genes are switched — necessarily over hours.

Reasoning · why are these receptors inside the cell?

Location follows the ligand's chemistry. Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble and cross the plasma membrane freely, so there is no need for a surface receptor to detect them — the receptor can sit in the cytoplasm or nucleus, right next to the DNA it will regulate. A water-soluble transmitter could never do this, which is why ionotropic and GPCR ligands stay outside.

Clinical / real-world

This class includes some of medicine's workhorses: glucocorticoids (prednisolone) for inflammation, oestrogen/anti-oestrogens (tamoxifen blocks the oestrogen receptor in breast cancer), anti-androgens for prostate cancer, and thyroid hormone replacement. Because they act by changing gene expression, onset is slow and effects are broad — explaining both the delay in steroid benefit and the wide side-effect profile of long-term steroids.

§2.5Receptor heterogeneity, subtypes & allosteric modulation

Within each family, receptors come in subtypes — mostly different genes encoding distinct receptors with similar architecture but significant differences in sequence and, often, pharmacology. This is the basis of drug selectivity: a drug can be built to prefer one subtype over another.

Label Key — same fold, different detail
7 transmembrane domains
All three are GPCRs with the same seven-helix plan (NH₂ out, COOH in) — the shared architecture.
Sequence differences (loops/termini)
The intracellular loops and C-terminal tails differ between α1A, α2A and β1 — small changes that alter G-protein coupling and drug binding.
Consequence
Different subtypes → different tissues and responses (α1 vasoconstriction, β1 cardiac stimulation), so a subtype-selective drug can target one and spare the others.
Label Key — orthosteric vs allosteric, across the board
Orthosteric ligand
Binds the receptor's natural site to activate it directly. The reference point.
Allosteric ligand
Binds a different site and changes the response — enhancing or reducing it — without being the primary activator. Shown for all four families.
Why it matters
Allosteric drugs offer a ceiling (they only work when the natural ligand is present) and finer selectivity, since allosteric sites are less conserved than orthosteric ones.

Plate 2.11 shows why selectivity is even possible — subtypes share a fold but differ in detail — and Plate 2.12 shows a second lever: every superfamily can be tuned from an allosteric site (recall the benzodiazepine site of §2.1 is exactly this). Together they explain how modern drugs achieve precision: pick the right subtype, and modulate rather than fully switch.

Reasoning · why allosteric modulation is often safer

An orthosteric agonist works everywhere the receptor is, all the time. An allosteric modulator only shifts the response to the endogenous ligand — so it acts where and when the body is already signalling, preserving natural rhythm and giving a built-in ceiling (you can't over-drive a receptor that has no natural ligand present). Allosteric sites are also less conserved between subtypes, so they can be more selective.

Clinical / real-world

Subtype selectivity is everyday prescribing: β1-selective beta-blockers (atenolol) spare the airway β2 receptors, safer in asthma; salbutamol targets β2 to bronchodilate. Allosteric modulation gives the benzodiazepines their favourable safety margin (§2.1) and underlies newer drugs like the calcium-sensing-receptor modulator cinacalcet.

§2.6Functional selectivity (biased agonism)

A single receptor often couples to more than one downstream pathway. Functional selectivity — also called biased agonism — is when an agonist preferentially drives one of those pathways over another, instead of activating them in the usual proportion.

Label Key — reading the two panels
A · Conventional agonism
Both agonists drive Response 1 and Response 2 in the same balance — the "unbiased" default.
B · Biased agonism
One agonist favours Response 1 (thick arrow) while the other favours Response 2 — same receptor, different downstream emphasis (e.g. G-protein vs β-arrestin).
Why it matters
If the therapeutic effect and the side effect run through different pathways, a biased agonist could give one without the other.

Plate 2.13 connects back to §2.2: because a GPCR can signal through both its G-protein and β-arrestin (Plate 2.6), an agonist that favours one arm is "biased". The therapeutic dream is to keep the wanted effect and drop the harmful one by choosing the pathway.

Reasoning · how can one receptor pick a pathway?

Different agonists stabilise subtly different receptor conformations. Each conformation couples better to some transducers (G-protein) than others (β-arrestin), so the shape a ligand imposes decides which downstream road is favoured. The receptor is not a simple on/off switch but a molecule with several signalling faces.

Clinical / real-world

The headline example is opioids: analgesia is thought to run mainly through G-protein signalling while respiratory depression and constipation involve β-arrestin. A G-protein-biased μ-opioid agonist (oliceridine) was developed to try to keep the pain relief while reducing the dangerous respiratory depression — biased agonism as a drug-design strategy.

R Recall checklist — the four receptor superfamilies
  • Type 1 ionotropic — nicotinic ACh / GABA_A / NMDA; 4–5 subunits round a pore; effector = the channel; milliseconds.
  • Type 2 GPCR — 7-TM; couples via G-protein (α,β,γ); GTPase in α; Gs↑ / Gi↓ adenylyl cyclase, Gq → PLC; seconds.
  • G-protein cycle — agonist drives GDP→GTP exchange (on); α-GTPase hydrolyses GTP (off).
  • Desensitisation — GRK → β-arrestin → clathrin internalisation → recycle or degrade (⇒ tolerance).
  • Type 3 kinase-linked — insulin/growth factors/cytokines; dimerise + autophosphorylate; RTK→Ras→Raf→MEK→MAPK; cytokine→JAK-STAT; hours.
  • Type 4 nuclear — steroid/thyroid; ligand-activated transcription factors; class I cytoplasm (on HSP), class II nucleus; bind HRE; hours.
  • Selectivity levers — subtypes (α1A/α2A/β1), allosteric modulation (all 4 families), functional selectivity / biased agonism.
§3L10 slides 15–21 · Objective: transporters as targets

Transporters as drug targets

Carriers for what can't cross alone — and the drugs that block them.

Transporters (also called carriers) exist because many important molecules are insufficiently lipid-soluble to cross membranes on their own. They ferry ions and organic molecules across the body's key barriers — the renal tubule, the intestinal epithelium and the blood-brain barrier. Where a carrier controls a molecule's movement, a drug can control that carrier — which is how a large slice of neuropharmacology (and the diuretics, and much drug handling) works.

Label Key — the transport modes
Passive / facilitated diffusion
Downhill, no energy: solute moves from high to low electrochemical potential; facilitated diffusion just uses a carrier to speed it. Sets the baseline "free" movement.
Symport
Secondary active: two solutes carried the same direction, one running downhill to drag the other uphill.
Antiport
Secondary active: two solutes carried in opposite directions, again using one gradient to power the other.
Primary active transport (ATP → ADP)
Uses ATP hydrolysis directly to move solute uphill (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) — the ultimate source of the gradients the secondary carriers exploit.

Plate 3.1 sorts transport by energy source. Passive/facilitated diffusion coasts down the gradient; secondary active transport (symport/antiport) borrows an existing ion gradient; and primary active transport spends ATP to build gradients in the first place. The Na+/K+ pump is the archetypal primary pump — and, indirectly, the engine behind the secondary carriers.

Reasoning · why bother with secondary active transport?

Making ATP-driven pumps for every solute would be wasteful. Instead the cell spends ATP once (mainly on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) to set up a steep Na⁺ gradient, then re-uses that stored energy over and over: symporters and antiporters let Na⁺ flow "downhill" back in and harness it to haul glucose, amino acids or other ions "uphill". One expensive pump powers many cheap carriers — an energy economy.

Two carrier superfamilies: SLC and ABC

Label Key — SLC in drug disposition
SLC transporters
The solute-carrier superfamily: they facilitate transport down the electrochemical gradient. Include the neurotransmitter reuptake carriers (SERT, NET, DAT).
Drug transport / metabolism
SLCs carry drugs into cells, feeding drug metabolism and delivering the drug to its target (MoA).
Cytotoxicity
Uptake can also concentrate a toxin inside the cell — the "false substrate accumulation" idea from §0 applied to carriers.

As Plate 3.2 shows, the SLC carriers do more than move a physiological solute down its gradient: the same facilitated route pulls drugs into the cell, so one transporter can feed drug metabolism, deliver an agent to its intracellular target, or — with a toxin — drive cytotoxicity by concentrating it inside.

Label Key — the ABC efflux cycle
ABC transporter
ATP-Binding Cassette family: transports substances against their gradient using the energy of ATP hydrolysis — i.e. primary active transport.
NBD1 / NBD2
The two nucleotide-binding domains that grip and hydrolyse ATP; their closing/opening drives the conformational change that moves substrate.
Interior → exterior
Substrate is pumped out of the cell (efflux). P-glycoprotein is the classic example — it throws drugs back out.

As Plate 3.3 shows, an ABC transporter works in the opposite direction and at a cost: its two nucleotide-binding domains grip and hydrolyse ATP, and that closing-and-opening cycle powers a conformational change that pumps the substrate from interior to exterior — primary active efflux, exactly the move P-glycoprotein uses to throw drugs back out. Taken together, Plates 3.2 and 3.3 contrast the two carrier families the deck names: SLC carriers move solutes down their gradient (facilitated) and bring drugs in, while ABC transporters burn ATP to pump substances out. P-glycoprotein (an ABC pump) matters enormously for drugs because it effluxes them from cells.

Clinical / real-world

P-glycoprotein at the gut, blood-brain barrier and tumour cells throws drugs back out, so it limits oral absorption, keeps drugs out of the brain, and — when over-expressed by cancer cells — causes multidrug resistance to chemotherapy. It is also a source of drug interactions (a P-gp inhibitor can raise levels of a P-gp substrate such as digoxin). SLC carriers matter too: the renal OAT/OCT transporters handle drug excretion (probenecid famously blocks penicillin secretion).

§3.1Transporter inhibitors: reuptake blockers in the CNS

Many CNS drugs act by inhibiting the reuptake of neurotransmitters, which increases neurotransmission by leaving more transmitter in the synapse. The antidepressants are the flagship group: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs). Psychomotor stimulants hit the same carriers: cocaine inhibits dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake; amphetamines inhibit dopamine and noradrenaline uptake; MDMA inhibits serotonin uptake (each with additional mechanisms).

Label Key — transporters and their inhibitors
NET (noradrenaline transporter)
Recaptures released NE back into the noradrenergic terminal (reuptake). Blocked by TCAs and SNRIs, raising synaptic NE.
SERT (serotonin transporter)
Recaptures released 5-HT into the serotonergic terminal. Blocked by SSRIs, TCAs and SNRIs, raising synaptic 5-HT — the antidepressant mechanism.
MAO (monoamine oxidase)
The intracellular enzyme that degrades recaptured monoamines; blocked by MAOIs — an enzyme target working alongside the transporter targets.
α₂AR autoreceptor
Presynaptic brake: released NE feeds back through α₂ to reduce further release — the system's own governor.
Li⁺ (lithium)
Acts downstream on the postsynaptic IP₃/PIP₂ second-messenger cycle, modulating signalling — a mood-stabiliser example beyond simple reuptake.

Plate 3.4 ties the whole guide together in one picture: transporters (SERT, NET) are blocked by SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs, an enzyme (MAO) is blocked by MAOIs, and GPCRs (α2, β, 5-HT receptors) read the resulting signal — three target classes on one synapse. Blocking reuptake keeps transmitter in the cleft longer, boosting transmission without making more transmitter.

Reasoning · why block reuptake instead of adding transmitter?

Reuptake is the main way a monoamine signal is switched off. Inhibit the transporter and each molecule of naturally released transmitter acts for longer and diffuses further — you amplify the brain's own signalling pattern rather than blanketing every synapse with exogenous transmitter. Same "amplify what's happening" logic as the anticholinesterases in §1.1, now applied to a carrier instead of an enzyme.

Memory hook · name says the target

SSRI = Serotonin-Selective Reuptake Inhibitor (SERT). SNRI adds Noradrenaline (SERT + NET). MAOI hits the enzyme MAO, not a transporter. The acronym literally spells the mechanism.

Clinical / real-world

Because SSRIs raise synaptic 5-HT, combining serotonergic drugs (an SSRI + an MAOI, or + tramadol) risks serotonin syndrome — agitation, hyperthermia, clonus. TCAs also block muscarinic, histamine and α-receptors, explaining their anticholinergic side effects and danger in overdose (cardiac sodium-channel block). Knowing which carrier/enzyme each class hits predicts both the therapeutic effect and the interaction risks.

R Recall checklist — transporters
  • Why carriers? — move poorly lipid-soluble solutes across renal tubule, gut epithelium, blood-brain barrier.
  • Passive (downhill, no ATP) vs active (uphill); secondary = symport/antiport on an ion gradient; primary = ATP directly (Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
  • SLC — facilitate transport down the gradient (SERT/NET/DAT, drug uptake).
  • ABC — ATP-driven efflux (P-glycoprotein → poor absorption, BBB exclusion, multidrug resistance).
  • Reuptake inhibitors — SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs block SERT/NET; cocaine/amphetamine/MDMA hit DAT/NET/SERT; MAOIs block the enzyme MAO.
§4L10 slide 22 · Conclusion

Tying it together

One grid explains every drug in the unit.

Return to Plate 0.1 with everything from §1–§3 in hand and it reads differently: the same three actions — activate, inhibit/block, modulate — cover receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters. Every specific drug you met is one square of that grid: an anticholinesterase inhibits an enzyme; a benzodiazepine modulates an ion channel; an SSRI inhibits a transporter; an opioid activates a receptor.

The unit on one page — target class, tempo and a drug
Target classSpeedAction in the deckExample drug
EnzymeFast (no transcription)Inhibit / false substrateDonepezil (AChE); methotrexate (DHFR)
Ion channel (Type 1 receptor)MillisecondsBlock / modulateDiazepam (GABA_A modulator); memantine (NMDA blocker)
GPCR (Type 2)SecondsAgonise / antagoniseMorphine (μ-opioid); atenolol (β1)
Kinase-linked (Type 3)HoursInhibit the kinaseImatinib; trastuzumab; tofacitinib
Nuclear (Type 4)HoursAgonise / antagonise transcriptionPrednisolone; tamoxifen
TransporterFast (block reuptake)InhibitSSRIs (SERT); loop diuretics (renal carriers)
Reasoning · the target predicts the behaviour

Once you know a drug's target class you can predict a lot without memorising it: an ionotropic or enzyme action is fast; a kinase-linked or nuclear action is slow because it works through transcription; and side effects follow whether the drug removes a normal product (block) or creates an abnormal one (false substrate). The four axes — location, effector, coupling, structure — are the questions that decode any new drug.

Clinical / real-world

Selectivity is what makes a target useful: pick the right receptor subtype (β1 not β2), the right carrier (SERT not NET), or use allosteric/biased action to keep the wanted response and drop the harmful one. This is the through-line from a nerve-gas poisoning to a modern biased opioid — same grid, better aim.

R Recall checklist — whole guide
  • 4 target classes × 3 actions — receptors / channels / enzymes / transporters, each activated, inhibited or modulated.
  • Enzymes — inhibitors & false substrates; AChE (reversible vs irreversible); antifolates (methotrexate, 5-FU).
  • 4 receptor superfamilies — ionotropic (ms) / GPCR (s) / kinase-linked (h) / nuclear (h); speed follows mechanism.
  • GPCR detail — 7-TM, G-protein cycle (GTPase in α), Gs/Gi/Gq + βγ, GRK/β-arrestin desensitisation.
  • Selectivity — subtypes, allosteric modulation, functional selectivity / biased agonism.
  • Transporters — passive vs active (secondary symport/antiport, primary ATP); SLC uptake vs ABC/P-gp efflux; reuptake inhibitors (SSRI/SNRI/TCA).
